newsitem.title: USA: American Air returns to skies after Clinton rescue.
newsitem.headline: American Air returns to skies after Clinton rescue.

text.p: American Airlines, rescued from a devastating pilots' strike by President Bill Clinton, slashed fares on Saturday to win back jittery passengers as its planes returned to the skies.

The nation's second-largest carrier had almost all of its domestic flights running on schedule again on Saturday morning and was wooing wary travelers with a half-price sale on domestic and international flights.
Many passengers who feared they would be left stranded were delighted, some whooping with joy as they boarded planes to start their vacations.
"This is great. I was sure we were going to lose out but, hey, here we are, on our way to Honolulu," passenger Jack Moran said at American's home Dallas-Fort Worth airport. "Life is good again."

American officials said that system-wide their domestic flights were running about 58 percent full, down about 10 points from where it would usually be over the long Presidents Day holiday weekend but still way above expectations.
"I guess an awful lot of people had faith that their flights would operate today," spokesman Rob Britton said. "It would have been a nightmare if there had been a strike."

American, a unit of Fort Worth-based AMR Corp, carries 20 percent of U.S. air travelers and a grounding of its 2,200 daily flights had been expected to cause havoc in the Caribbean, which is in its peak winter holiday season, and in cities across the country where American is strong.

Union leaders ordered all 9,300 American pilots to walk off the job at midnight on Friday (0500 GMT on Saturday) after five days of intense negotiations with management failed to bring agreement on a new four-year labor contract.

But Clinton stepped in within minutes, using emergency powers to appoint a presidential board which will study the dispute and draw up a proposed solution within 30 days. Both sides will then have 30 days to respond.
Clinton's move effectively forced the pilots back to work just 24 minutes after they had launched their strike, and postponed any new walkout for 60 days.
Union leaders said they were not pleased by Clinton's intervention and warned the dispute was still far from over.

Other American workers, however, were delighted. Skycaps and other workmates hugged one another and slapped each other's backs as they arrived for morning shifts at Miami International Airport on Saturday.
A pilots strike would have cost American upwards of $30 million a day and the U.S. economy $100-200 million a day.

Just the threat of a walkout had already caused major disruption to the U.S. air travel system, sending tens of thousands of passengers scrambling to change their bookings from American ahead of the three-day Presidents Day weekend.

"It was a nightmare. It was a total nightmare," Jennifer Hyde, 27, said of her struggles to guarantee a Saturday flight to Panama City from Miami. Smiling broadly, she said she had doublebooked with another airline to avoid being stranded but was delighted the strike was over because she could now use her cheaper American ticket.
Other passengers, however, did not switch back to American and airline president Don Carty said the net loss to from the run-up to the strike was about $100 million.
Moving quickly to win back disillusioned passengers, American announced heavy sales and promotions just minutes after Clinton stopped the striking pilots in their tracks.
They included discounts of 50 percent and more on domestic and international flights with no advance purchase requirements, and a doubling of frequent flier mile credits.

For example, American's Los Angeles-Chicago round trip fare for travel before March 14 was slashed from $889 to $388 and the Boston-Chicago round trip fare was dropped to $238 to $493. On its international service, the New York-London fare dropped almost 50 percent to $238 and the Dallas-Paris fare was halved to $389.
Cargo customers were offered discounts of 45 percent.
American officials said they fully expected rival carriers to match the offers.
